pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
STATEMENT OF STACEY BURBURE 
AMERICAN ELECTRIC POWER COMPANY, INC. 
PANEL 1 
 
American Electric Power Company, Inc. (“AEP”) appreciates the opportunity to participate 
on Panel 1 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission” or “FERC”) technical 
conference on governance and stakeholder reforms in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”).1 As 
Senior Vice President of Transmission Regulatory Engagement and Compliance, I support AEP’s 
operating utilities, including those operating within the PJM region. AEP operates within seven of 
the thirteen states in PJM’s footprint (Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Tennessee, Virginia, and 
West Virginia).   
AEP participates in four Regional Transmission Organizations (“RTO”): PJM, the 
Midcontinent Independent System Operator (“MISO”), the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”), and 
the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”), providing the company with broad 
experience across diverse governance models, market structures, and planning frameworks. In 
addition to my responsibilities supporting AEP’s utilities across these regions, I serve on the SPP 
Members Committee, providing firsthand experience with RTO stakeholder governance and 
decision-making.  
 
 
1 The questions posed by the Commission to Panel 1 and AEP’s answers are set forth in the Appendix to this statement.

2 
I. 
Introduction and Summary 
The United States has before it today one of the greatest requirements for energy 
development in generations. This required energy development is largely driven by the national 
interest in being the worldwide leader in artificial intelligence infrastructure and technology. 
Addressing this national interest is essential to national security and presents a tremendous 
opportunity to drive economic growth. At its core, AEP’s concern with PJM is that it is 
dysfunctional, ineffective, and not capable of doing its job of supporting the deployment of 
massive amounts of needed generation and transmission by its members. In short, PJM is broken 
and must be immediately fixed. 
To avoid the catastrophic effects of jeopardizing our national security and economic growth, 
PJM must immediately change. PJM must change its operations and governance to allow 
customers to interconnect load and generation faster. PJM must have a planning process that takes 
transmission and generation into account together. That planning process must identify and provide 
sufficient resources to meet the needs of existing and future customers. Finally, PJM governance 
must change so stakeholders can be heard, innovation can occur, decisions can be made, and PJM 
can move forward and get out of the deadlock it faces today.  
AEP proposes three overarching areas of change for PJM. First, generator interconnection 
must be reformed in PJM. Under current interconnection rules, a generator cannot reach 
commercial operation without significant delays and inefficiencies. This discourages generation 
development. Second, PJM’s approach to ensuring resource adequacy in the region must be 
updated. PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model has failed to send efficient investment and retirement 
signals which has distorted price formation. The result is diminished long-term revenue certainty 
for generation developers which discourages investment in dependable, dispatchable generation 
and undermines resource adequacy over time. Third, PJM governance and stakeholder processes

3 
must be reformed. PJM is seeking to solve today’s challenges with an outdated Board of Managers 
(“Board”) governance and stakeholder process where necessary reforms cannot be implemented 
efficiently and effectively.  Too often, reforms are stymied by a stakeholder process that 
consistently deadlocks on important issues and a Board governance model lacking clear 
accountability and the will to drive change.  
The need for change in these three areas is urgent. PJM is confronting the most significant 
reliability, affordability, and infrastructure challenge in its history. Demand from national security 
needs, advanced manufacturing, data centers, and electrification is accelerating faster than the 
region is able to plan and build the infrastructure needed to support it through PJM’s current 
mechanisms. The question before the Commission is whether PJM’s Board governance structure 
and stakeholder process enable timely, technically sound decisions that maintain reliability, 
support affordability, and enable economic growth. In AEP’s view, they do not.  
PJM suffers from a governance mismatch: responsibility for outcomes rests with the Board, 
but authority over many of the tools needed to achieve those outcomes remains fragmented. PJM’s 
existing governance framework has not consistently enabled timely action to meet customer needs 
or address evolving reliability, planning, and market challenges. That is not a sustainable near-term 
or long-term operating condition for the region. PJM’s governance structure must align 
responsibility, authority, and accountability so that those charged with ensuring reliability have the 
ability—and the obligation—to deliver it. PJM states, accountable to their citizens, lack any formal 
role. While every stakeholder deserves a voice, governance must better reflect who is responsible 
for planning, financing, operating, and maintaining the infrastructure upon which reliability 
depends, and solving the urgent generator interconnection and resource adequacy issues.

4 
Effective governance is not measured by the number of committees or the degree of 
stakeholder participation. It is measured by whether responsibility, authority, and accountability 
are aligned to produce timely decisions that maintain reliability, support affordability, and enable 
fast generation interconnection to support national security and economic growth. It is ultimately 
measured by customer outcomes: Do the lights stay on, is growth supported on the customer’s 
development timeline, and do planning processes stay ahead of demand so growth can occur and 
important national interests like security and AI development can move forward unconstrained? 
Reliable, affordable, and efficient customer service form the foundation of AEP’s 
recommendations.  
II. 
How Process Thwarts Substance in PJM—An Illustration 
Today’s stakeholder process makes it nearly impossible to evaluate integrated solutions 
that span the two areas most critically in need of change—generation interconnection and resource 
adequacy—as well as related areas of load interconnection and market design. A reformed process 
must enable stakeholders to bring creative proposals designed to solve PJM’s biggest problems to 
the table for serious review by other stakeholders, PJM management, and the Board.  
The current PJM stakeholder process does not encourage new innovative ideas and the 
structure of the committee system complicates needed market reforms that hope to solve some of 
today’s greatest challenges. As far back as December of 2024, the PJM Board publicly 
acknowledged that they foresaw immediate capacity shortage conditions in the 2026/27 Delivery 
Year forecast. With an unprecedented challenge that should have prompted bold action, PJM 
proposed only minor changes.  This was, in part, due to the byzantine nature of the stakeholder 
process and an inability to bring about consensus from its membership. When faced with today’s 
unprecedented challenges, AEP believes that instead of minor tweaks, PJM should be empowered

5 
to move forward boldly with solutions which may not gain the support of entrenched market 
participants who benefit from the status quo. 
One such proposal that helps to demonstrate this archaic stakeholder misalignment within 
the PJM governance process is AEP’s Accelerated Load, Infrastructure, Generation and Network 
Planning (“ALIGN”) concept. AEP’s ALIGN concept is for PJM to consolidate planning so that 
committed load, generation resources, and transmission facilities would be planned and evaluated 
as a coordinated portfolio rather than through separate and sequential processes. Eligibility would 
be limited to projects supported by executed agreements, financial security, and other enforceable 
commitments, thereby helping distinguish executable projects from speculative queue activity. 
ALIGN would also augment PJM’s existing planning and interconnection processes, not replace 
them. By concentrating planning studies on committed demand, the framework is intended to 
improve queue integrity, increase planning certainty, and better align infrastructure investment 
with actual customer need. 
AEP’s ALIGN proposal illustrates why governance reform matters: today’s stakeholder 
process could require the proposal to be fragmented across multiple committees and multiple filing 
authorities before its merits could even be evaluated. Despite working as an integrated framework, 
the proposal could be broken up among stakeholder groups focusing on generator interconnection, 
load interconnection, transmission planning, and others where aspects would be debated in 
isolation. Then, if the proposal advanced, because it would require both Tariff and Operating 
Agreement revisions, a two-sector Members Committee veto could block the whole concept. A 
well-formed stakeholder process must not stifle big, innovative ideas; it must facilitate their 
consideration on the merits.

6 
AEP’s ALIGN concept is not without precedent. Other RTOs have been able to 
successfully incorporate and demonstrate the value of integrated planning processes that evaluate 
multiple infrastructure needs together rather than through disconnected stakeholder processes. SPP 
was able to incorporate its Integrated Transmission Planning process which evaluates reliability, 
economic, and public policy needs within a single coordinated planning framework. ALIGN 
applies that same planning philosophy to today’s emerging challenges and takes it one step further. 
Rather than evaluating committed load, generation, and transmission through separate 
interconnection queues, planning processes, and stakeholder committees, ALIGN would enable 
PJM to evaluate these interdependent facilities as a coordinated infrastructure portfolio.  
The lesson is not that PJM should replicate another RTO’s planning process. Rather, it is 
that governance must enable planners and stakeholders to evaluate comprehensive infrastructure 
solutions that reflect how the electric system actually functions. As load growth accelerates and 
infrastructure development becomes increasingly complex, PJM’s governance structure must 
evolve to support the innovation that will be required to meet the needs of today and the next 
century. The purpose of governance reform is to enable technically superior solutions by aligning 
responsibility, authority, and accountability.  
III. 
PJM And Its Stakeholders: Reform Is Needed To Facilitate Action 
PJM’s immediate market and planning issues must be addressed through the most effective 
near-term mechanisms available, but the underlying governance deficiencies also must be 
addressed to place PJM, its members, and its states on a more durable path. A stakeholder 
framework that clearly allocates responsibility, facilitates the Board’s work, and enables timely 
Commission review will better support the Board’s independence, responsiveness, and ability to 
act—producing better results for reliability, infrastructure development, and market reforms over 
the long term.

7 
Specifically, AEP recommends PJM create an advisory stakeholder structure aligning the 
advisory function with an appropriate process to enable stakeholders to provide better, actionable 
advice to the Board. This will restore balance to PJM’s governance structure and unlock the 
Board’s ability to make decisions and address the most important issues proactively, nimbly, and 
decisively. 
While an advisory stakeholder process and an empowered board are ideas borrowed from 
some other RTOs’ approaches, PJM’s size, diversity of states, and range of regulatory paradigms 
distinguish it. The Commission’s mantra—that one-size-fits-all approaches do not work—rings 
true here. AEP’s goal is not for PJM to adopt any particular structure for its own sake, but to 
achieve a balance that is fair and sensible for all stakeholders, including by appropriately reflecting 
the interests of parties with responsibility for, and exposure to, reliability and cost impacts in the 
region. And critically, PJM needs a structure that enables the Board to make timely decisions in 
support of national security, reliability, affordability, and economic development.  
IV. 
The Role of the States  
States must have a voice in PJM’s stakeholder process and revised governance structure. 
As to the role of states in PJM processes, AEP is steadfastly supportive of proposals that result in 
a governance framework that is balanced and appropriately reflects the interests of parties with 
responsibility for—and exposure to—reliability and cost impacts in the region. The central 
objective of this and other governance reforms must be ensuring that PJM is able to achieve the 
core goals of regional coordination: transmission system reliability and “an abundant supply of 
electric energy … with the greatest possible economy.”2  AEP supports providing states with 
 
2 16 U.S.C. § 824a(a); see Federal Power Act; Delegation of Authority to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 
63 Fed. Reg. 53889-01 (Oct. 7, 1998) (delegating Section 202(a) authority to FERC and noting that such authority 
“could aid in … addressing reliability-related issues, thereby increasing the reliability of the transmission system”).

8 
defined authority under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act to cause filings to be made before 
the Commission on matters within their collective jurisdiction, recognizing that states have a direct 
responsibility for protecting consumers and advancing resource adequacy, affordability, and public 
policy objectives. 
Today, there is a mismatch between which entities have responsibility for reliability, 
resource adequacy, and cost impacts, and which are able to control or influence PJM decisions that 
directly affect those outcomes. Governance reform efforts—including rethinking the role of states 
in PJM—must seek to bridge this gap.   
V. 
The Role of the Board 
AEP recommends targeted modifications to PJM’s governance rules that would strengthen 
the PJM Board’s effectiveness while preserving its independence and responsiveness. 
• PJM must adopt a preference for Board candidates who reside within the PJM 
footprint and have significant professional experience with the region’s electric 
system.  
• PJM’s Operating Agreement must be revised to make the President and CEO a 
voting member of the Board. Under current rules, PJM’s President and CEO sits on 
the Board ex officio, but does not have a vote.3   
• PJM’s ex parte rules must be amended to eliminate or significantly reduce limits 
on communications between the Board and stakeholders. Reforming PJM’s ex 
parte rules would improve governance by enabling Board members to receive 
timely, balanced, and informed perspectives on complex national security, 
reliability, market, and transmission planning issues. 
 
3 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.1.

9 
VI. 
Conclusion 
PJM stakeholders—from transmission owners and generators to states and consumer 
advocates—are committed to serving customers across the region reliably, at least cost. But too 
often, PJM’s governance structure has inhibited, rather than facilitated, this essential work. Action 
takes too long, even as problems proliferate, and the solutions adopted do not meet the moment. 
PJM’s structure handcuffs the Board from leading from the front and mires stakeholders with 
process over substance. “[T]he status quo,” as Chairman Swett has put it, “is unacceptable and has 
been for some time.”4  To secure the greatest benefits for the 67 million customers who rely on 
PJM, the Board must be able to act proactively, nimbly, and decisively with useful input from 
stakeholders to solve the region’s challenges.  
PJM’s governance structure was developed for a different era—one characterized by 
slower load growth, excess generation, and incremental infrastructure needs. Today’s environment 
is fundamentally different. Meeting the nation’s growing demand for electricity will require an 
RTO capable of making timely, informed, and accountable decisions. Governance reform must 
not seek to diminish stakeholder participation, but rather ensure that stakeholder engagement 
produces actionable advice, that the Board possesses the authority necessary to fulfill its statutory 
responsibilities, and that states have a meaningful voice in the process. The next generation of grid 
challenges will not be solved by incremental procedural reforms. They will require governance 
capable of evaluating integrated technical solutions such as ALIGN, empowering the Board to act, 
incorporating meaningful stakeholder and state input, and aligning responsibility, authority and 
accountability.  
 
 
4  FERC, Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, Md. (May 12, 2026), 
https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/chairman-laura-swetts-comments-pjms-annual-meeting-baltimore-md-0.

10 
In summary, PJM is broken and must be fixed one way or the other. Our national security 
and ability to satisfy customer requirements are at risk. The current precarious state of affairs must 
be addressed immediately. 
Respectfully,  
 
/s/ Stacey Burbure  
Stacey Burbure  
SVP, Transmission Regulatory Engagement and Compliance  
American Electric Power  
8500 Smith’s Mill Road  
New Albany, OH 43054

1 
 
APPENDIX 
PANEL 1 QUESTIONS 
1. What is the PJM Board’s role in ensuring that PJM is sufficiently tackling the region’s 
operational and market challenges? How does the Board evaluate its effectiveness in 
that role? How often, and under what circumstances, does the Board act unilaterally, 
and should this change? 
 
The resource adequacy challenges facing PJM are existential. Its fundamental charge is to 
serve customers reliably. Despite a half-decade of lead time, the issue is still not under control. 
This struggle has revealed that the Board lacks a consistent ability to take timely action to meet 
customer needs or address evolving national security matters, reliability, planning, and market 
challenges. The Board has been forced to be reactive and defensive rather than nimble and decisive, 
preventing timely action. AEP believes the cause is an imbalance among the core goals that RTOs 
under Order No. 2000 must pursue: independence, responsiveness, and action. 
Independence. Independence is the “bedrock upon which [PJM] must be built,”5 requiring 
the RTO to maintain “a decision making process that is independent of control by any market 
participant or class of participants.” 6  PJM’s Board is structurally independent, but it lacks 
functional independence, impeding decision making.7  A well-functioning Board must have the 
expertise, confidence and backbone to make hard decisions that will have significant impacts and 
draw opposition. Those decisions, however, need not and must not be made in isolation; they must 
be made based on experience, a robust understanding of the substance, and full consideration of 
diverse stakeholders’ needs. This can only be achieved when Board members can engage on the 
 
5 Reg’l Transmission Orgs., Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089 at 31,046 (1999), order on reh’g, Order 
No. 2000-A, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,092 (2000) (cleaned up). 
6 Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089 at 31,060. 
7 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 96 FERC ¶ 61,061 at 8 (2001).

2 
 
ground through committees where the work of the RTO is done, and through formal and informal 
discussions with stakeholders. PJM’s structure, however, limits these opportunities. 
Responsiveness. PJM must be “responsive[] to the needs of customers and other 
stakeholders,” providing “avenue[s] for customers and other stakeholders to present their views 
on RTO and ISO decision-making, and to have those views considered.” 8  Although PJM’s 
stakeholder process attempts to fulfill this requirement, 9  structural flaws in the Members 
Committee create gridlock and stalemate rather than useful input for the Board. As PJM’s most 
senior committee, the Members Committee reviews recommendations from all other committees 
and approves actions or recommendations with a two-thirds sector-weighted vote.10  The two-
thirds requirement is not just limited to amending the Operating Agreement, over which the 
Members Committee maintains Section 205 filing rights, but extends to any recommendations to 
the Board. But because there are five sectors, any two sectors can combine to veto an action. As 
recent history has shown,11 the Members Committee’s advice to the Board is far too often no 
advice at all. Moreover, because the stakeholder process is split across numerous committees, 
subcommittees, task forces, and other groups, stakeholders struggle to bring broad proposals to 
address cross-cutting issues.  
This leads to a situation where transmission owners and other entities which serve load are 
unable to be responsive to customer needs, such as by fostering processes that allow new load and 
generation to get connected in the time the customer needs, not an RTO-mandated timeline built 
 
8 Wholesale Competition in Regions with Organized Elec. Mkts., Order No. 719, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,281 at PP 
502-03 (2008), order on reh’g, Order No. 719-A, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,292 (2009). 
9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 133 FERC ¶ 61,071 at PP 1-2 (2010). 
10 PJM Operating Agreement § 8.4. 
11 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER24-98-000, Transmittal Letter. at 5, 63-64 (filed Oct. 13, 
2023).

3 
 
for another era. A case in point is the process for interconnecting generation to serve new loads. It 
is slow and iterative with long study timelines and repeated restudies. While action is being taken 
to improve this issue, those measures are only now being studied and do not mean that PJM has 
fully addressed the core governance issues causing its lack of responsiveness overall. 
Action. The Board’s “primary responsibility” under the Operating Agreement is to take 
action to ensure PJM is run in a manner “consistent with . . . the safe and reliable operation of the 
[] Region” and with a “robust, competitive, and non-discriminatory electric power market . . . .”12  
As the Commission has emphasized, RTO governance must facilitate effective action, so that the 
RTO can “ensure that [it] formulates policies, operates the system, and resolves disputes in a fair 
and non-discriminatory manner.” 13   And the Commission has stressed the need for RTO 
governance to be “workable.”14  But when the stakeholder process becomes a bottleneck, and the 
Board lacks the necessary authority, it becomes difficult for the Board to take action when needed. 
Exacerbating the challenges, the Members Committee holds Section 205 filing rights under the 
Operating Agreement not just for corporate issues of the RTO, but core functions like energy 
markets and regional transmission planning. Thus in many cases, the Board lacks the power to act 
on holistic solutions to the most pressing challenges outside of filing a Section 206 complaint. 
When issues were slow-moving and the region had surplus capacity, these challenges may 
have slipped under the radar—but this decade’s challenges have proved the status quo inadequate.

13 Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open Access Non-Discriminatory Transmission Servs. by Pub. Utils.; 
Recovery of Stranded Costs by Pub. Utils. & Transmitting Utils., Order No. 888, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,036 at 
31,731 (1996), order on reh’g, Order No. 888-A, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,048, order on reh’g, Order No. 888-B, 81 
FERC ¶ 61,248 (1997), order on reh’g, Order No. 888-C, 82 FERC ¶ 61,046 (1998), aff’d in relevant part sub nom. 
Transmission Access Pol’y Study Grp. v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667 (D.C. Cir. 2000), aff’d sub nom. New York v. FERC, 
535 U.S. 1 (2002). 
14 See, e.g., Order No. 719, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,281 at P 546; Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089 
at 31,065, 31,069, 31,076.

4 
 
A well-functioning Board, that is independent, responsive, willing to take action, and focused on 
the core RTO mission of maintaining reliability, supporting affordability, and enabling economic 
growth, would be better equipped to swiftly consider innovative approaches like AEP’s ALIGN 
concept than the current fragmented governance structure where passage requires that integrated 
ideas are rung through a time consuming gauntlet of lower level stakeholder committees.  
2. How should states, through the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (OPSI) or other 
structures, interface with the Board to enable the region to meet operational and 
market challenges while respecting PJM’s independence? 
 
States must have an expanded and more formal role in PJM’s governance process—
whether through state representation on the Board, creation of a state committee, or another 
structure—that provides states a meaningful voice while preserving PJM’s independence and fairly 
balancing the interests of parties with responsibility for grid reliability and cost impacts.  In Order 
No. 2000, the Commission recognized that “states have important roles to play in RTO matters,” 
but concluded that imposing “specific requirements on the role of state agencies in RTOs … would 
be counterproductive in light of the variation in the legal responsibilities of state commissions and 
RTO design across regions.”15  States have a key interest in reliable and affordable electric service 
for their citizens. These issues have become critically important challenges within the PJM region 
and are directly impacted by PJM decisions and policies. Yet states do not have any formal role in 
PJM governance, either individually or via the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (“OPSI”). States 
should be able to act as a key voice in promoting innovative, integrated solutions that they see as 
valuable for addressing today’s issues. With a more direct role in the stakeholder process, states 
could provide needed clarity to drive solutions—like ALIGN and similar integrated solutions that 
 
15 Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089 at 31,212, 31,073.

5 
 
we have seen in other RTOs—that span multiple stakeholder groups in transmission planning, 
generation interconnection, load interconnection, and market design.  
A variety of reform options could help right-size the role of states in PJM’s governance 
process. AEP offers two ideas. For example, the advisory stakeholder model discussed above 
would give states the opportunity to directly contribute to PJM policymaking processes. Indeed, 
one of the main benefits of the advisory process approach is that it would give a meaningful voice 
to states and other stakeholders who lack voting rights on the Members Committee.  
An expanded state role must be accompanied by stakeholder process reforms aimed at the 
core goals of enabling timely, technically sound decisions that drive dramatically improved 
national security, maintain reliability, support affordability, and enable economic growth. OPSI 
commissioners have acknowledged to FERC that the PJM states have diverse regulatory 
environments and policy interests.16 Without additional stakeholder reforms, an expanded state 
role could lead to further gridlock, indecision, and regulatory uncertainty. 
3. What governance reforms would best improve accountability and responsiveness? 
An advisory stakeholder model would best improve accountability and responsiveness. A 
well-functioning and vibrant stakeholder process will support the Board in achieving the best 
outcomes. The stakeholder process, however, has become an end unto itself, becoming a forum for 
gridlock, not advice. AEP recommends that PJM employ an advisory model that provides 
stakeholders a meaningful opportunity to explore options, find consensus, and advise the Board 
without the risk of obstruction and stalemate.  
 
16 Fed. & State Current Issues Collaborative, Docket No. AD24-7-000, Transcript of the 7/27/2025 Meeting on RTO 
Governance/Resource Adequacy (posted Aug. 25, 2025).

6 
 
A key flaw today is misalignment between stakeholders’ advisory role (on the one hand) 
and the process (on the other). Stakeholders wear many hats, from advising the Board to exercising 
Section 205 rights over the Operating Agreement. But the Members Committee has (with limited 
exceptions) a single process for approving matters: a two-thirds sector-weighted vote.17  Changing 
PJM’s decision-making rules, and recommending tweaks to the capacity market, are governed by 
the same rules. Moreover, because there are five sectors, it just takes two to band together to veto 
action. And with no de minimis threshold for participation, small groups can form minority 
coalitions to defeat proposals supported by majorities of the stakeholders with core interests in 
reliability and affordability. Moreover, the current sectors do not accurately reflect accountability. 
For example, PJM states have no formal role, yet they are accountable to their citizens, all of whom 
are electric customers reliant on the PJM grid. Further, AEP owns over 20% of the assets in PJM 
and controls less than 2% of the vote in the stakeholder process. Both of these examples show the 
disconnect that exists in the current system. 
Meanwhile, because the Members Committee is responsible for deciding core corporate 
governance issues, it does not provide voting rights to some stakeholders with important voices, 
including states—even when the Members Committee is serving purely in an advisory function.18  
States have important interests, but they lack full representation in the stakeholder process. As a 
result, States have resorted to extraordinary means to ensure their interests are heard.19 
PJM must create an advisory stakeholder process aligning role and function. Such a process 
would provide stakeholders a robust and meaningful opportunity to review proposals, develop 
 
17 PJM Operating Agreement ¶ 8.4. 
18 See Memorandum of Understanding Between PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. and the Organization of PJM States, Inc. 
(June 8, 2005), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/agreements/opsi-pjm-memorandum.ashx. 
19 See, e.g., Commonwealth of Penn. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,066 at PP 1-2 (2025) (describing 
the complaint filed against PJM by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and subsequent settlement).

7 
 
alternatives, test ideas, and achieve consensus where it can be found. The structure would be 
flexible, ensuring matters can be carefully scrutinized by committees of stakeholders with 
particular interests or expertise, but enabling broader, integrated proposals to be reviewed as a 
whole. Stakeholder voting would not follow a formal voting procedure that controls outcomes. 
PJM management, instead, would develop proposals after stakeholder engagement, and the Board 
would determine whether to proceed, weighing stakeholder input and exercising accountability for 
the final decision. This approach would enhance stakeholder participation while enabling more 
timely decision-making and clearer accountability. Such a structure would also enable PJM to give 
a full voice to more stakeholders, including states, which have strong interests in PJM’s success 
but currently lack a voice on the Members Committee. It could also be flexible, enabling 
stakeholders to propose big ideas, such as AEP’s ALIGN concept, to address cross-cutting issues 
that today may be split up across numerous balkanized committees, subcommittees, task forces, 
and other groups. 
4. How does the division of Federal Power Act section 20520 filing rights among PJM, 
Transmission Owners, and the Members Committee affect PJM’s ability to act 
effectively and quickly, when warranted, to address operational and market needs? 
 
PJM’s Board holds Section 205 filing rights over the majority of PJM’s operational 
functions, including those in the Tariff21 and Reliability Assurance Agreement.22 But the Members 
Committee retains Section 205 authority over some of these issues that are addressed in the 
Operating Agreement, including energy markets and the Regional Transmission Expansion 
Planning Protocol.23 Here, gridlock in the Members Committee is a binding constraint and limits 
 
20 16 U.S.C. § 824d. 
21 PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff § 9.2(a); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., PJM Manual 34: PJM Stakeholder 
Process 19 (effective Sep. 25, 2025), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m34.pdf. 
22 See PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement § 16.4. 
23 See PJM Operating Agreement Sched. 1 (Energy Markets) and Sched. 6 (RTEP).

8 
 
PJM from solving important problems. This is especially troubling for energy market provisions, 
which are included verbatim in both the Tariff and Operating Agreement, requiring alignment 
across the Board and Members Committee. 24  With respect to market design, AEP supports 
providing states with defined authority under Section 205 to cause filings to be made before the 
Commission on matters within their collective jurisdiction, recognizing that states have a direct 
responsibility for protecting consumers and advancing resource adequacy, affordability, and public 
policy objectives.   
PJM’s current stakeholder sector composition no longer reflects the responsibilities of 
today’s electric system, as it assigns equal voting weight regardless of an entity’s accountability 
for reliability, investment obligations, or operational responsibility, resulting in governance 
outcomes that are disconnected from those most responsible for maintaining a reliable grid. Equal 
voting power, however, is not the same as balanced governance. Effective governance recognizes 
that parties bearing the greatest responsibility for maintaining reliable electric service should have 
a commensurate role in shaping the decisions for which they ultimately remain accountable. States 
are accountable to their citizens for affordability, reliability, economic development, and resource 
adequacy.  A governance structure that excludes them from meaningful participation ignores one 
of the principal governmental entities responsible for electric service. 
It is time to reexamine whether it is appropriate for the Members Committee to retain 
Section 205 authority over core functional matters. The practical effect of the current system is 
that a single integrated solution, like AEP’s ALIGN concept, can require approvals under multiple 
governing documents with different filing priorities. Process therefore becomes a barrier to 
technical innovation.  
 
24 Compare PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff Attach. K-Appendix with PJM Operating Agreement Sched. 1.

9 
 
5. To what extent do provisions in PJM’s Operating Agreement, Transmission Owner 
Agreement, Open Access Transmission Tariff, Reliability Assurance Agreement, or 
Manuals impede timely decision-making by PJM? 
 
The stakeholder process, which is subject to deadlock and delay, is the core issue impeding 
timely decision-making by PJM. As noted above, the Members Committee must not retain Section 
205 authority over core functional matters.  
6. Recognizing regional differences, are there lessons from other regional transmission 
organization/independent system operator (RTO/ISO) governance structures that 
PJM could reasonably adopt to improve its responsiveness to the region’s operational 
and market challenges? 
 
AEP recommends five targeted modifications to PJM’s governance rules that would 
strengthen the PJM Board’s effectiveness while preserving its independence and responsiveness. 
These recommendations—which draw on approaches adopted by other RTOs and ISOs to improve 
governance—are discussed in greater detail below. Collectively, these reforms would modernize 
PJM governance by strengthening the connection between Board oversight and operational 
execution, improving the Board’s understanding of the unique and varied conditions within the 
PJM region, expanding the pool of qualified Board candidates, protecting against entrenchment 
and status quo bias in the Board nomination process, and allowing the Board to engage 
productively with stakeholders to effectively guide PJM and confront the complex challenges 
facing the region’s electric industry today. The common lesson across other RTOs is not identical 
governance structures, but rather that governance must align responsibility, authority, and 
accountability while enabling innovation.  
Voting rights for PJM’s President and CEO. PJM’s Operating Agreement must be revised 
to make the President and CEO a voting member of the Board. Under current rules, PJM’s

10 
 
President and CEO sits on the Board ex officio, but does not have a vote.25  As the executive 
responsible for implementing Board decisions and managing the nation’s largest wholesale 
electricity market, PJM’s President and CEO offers unique operational expertise and 
accountability—and must be fully involved in Board decision-making.   
Indeed, the CEOs of MISO, SPP, and NYISO are voting members of their respective 
RTO/ISOs’ boards (subject to certain recusal limits).26 Giving PJM’s President and CEO a vote on 
the Board would make PJM more dynamic by improving information flow, enhancing Board 
debate, and making the President/CEO a decision-making partner.  
In-region preference for Board candidates. PJM must adopt a preference for Board 
candidates who reside within the PJM footprint or have significant professional experience with 
the region’s electric system. Although PJM’s Operating Agreement imposes certain minimum 
expertise requirements that the Board collectively must meet, it does not require or prioritize 
familiarity with the PJM region.27 Accordingly, few current Board members had ties to the PJM 
region before joining the Board. Because Board decisions directly affect national security, electric 
reliability, affordability, and economic development across the PJM footprint, regional knowledge 
must be recognized as an important qualification for Board members. Notably, both ISO-NE and 
NYISO currently have preferences for in-region directors.28 Regional knowledge is particularly 
important in PJM, which has a uniquely large and diverse footprint that includes both vertically 
integrated and restructured states with significant variation in local supply and demand dynamics. 
As PJM itself recognized in a 2011 filing, adding Board members “from the PJM region who are 
 
25 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.1. 
26 See MISO Transmission Owner Agreement, App’x F (“MISO Bylaws”), Art. IV § 4.1; MISO Bylaws Art. V § 5.4; 
SPP Bylaws § 4.2.1; NYISO Bylaws, Art. III § 3(a).  
27 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.2. 
28 See ISO-NE Participants Agreement § 9.2.2; NYISO Bylaws, Art. III § 2.

11 
 
familiar with the current practices and operations of PJM” “is beneficial and crucial to PJM’s 
continued success.”29 
Shorter cooling-off period for prospective Board members. Limiting PJM’s “cooling-off” 
period for prospective Board members to one year also would improve PJM’s ability to attract 
qualified Board candidates with relevant experience and local knowledge. PJM’s rules require at 
least a two-year gap between service as a director, officer, or employee of a PJM member (or an 
affiliate or related party) and election to the PJM Board.30  This restriction unnecessarily limits the 
pool of qualified candidates with recent industry experience. A one-year period would maintain 
Board independence31 while improving PJM’s ability to recruit members with current expertise. 
This adjustment would more closely align PJM’s governance rules with those of other RTOs. 
MISO in 2017 reduced its cooling-off period from two years to one, explaining that the longer 
restriction had “affected MISO’s ability to recruit Board candidates” as it could “often times create 
conflicts that … disqualify an individual from consideration.”32 ISO-NE and SPP have no cooling-
off periods for board members.33 
 
29 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER11-630-000, Transmittal Letter at 2 (filed Sep. 23, 2011) (explaining 
that “electing members to the Board from the PJM footprint” will allow PJM to “maximize local input” and avoid 
“expend[ing] time and resources seeking and training candidates who lack the PJM-specific expertise that adds 
significant value to the PJM Board”). 
30 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.2. 
31 See Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089 at 31,062 (explaining that FERC’s “focus” in evaluating 
financial independence “will be on current financial interests” (emphasis added)). 
32 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER17-686-000, Transmittal Letter at 8-9 (filed Dec. 28, 2016); 
see Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER17-686-000, Letter Order (issued Feb. 23, 2017). PJM 
reduced its cooling-off period from five years to two years in 2011, due to the challenges the protracted cooling-off 
period created in finding qualified Board candidates from the PJM region. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. 
ER11-630-000, Transmittal Letter at 2 (filed Sep. 23, 2011); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER11-630-000, 
Letter Order (Nov. 1, 2011). 
33 Instead, both ISO-NE and SPP impose restrictions on board members’ current relationships with and financial 
interest in market participants. See ISO-NE Participants Agreement § 9.3.1; ISO-NE Code of Conduct § 2.2; SPP 
Bylaws § 4.2.3.

12 
 
Reduce Board control over nomination process. PJM must limit the role incumbent Board 
members play in the Board nomination process. Under current rules, PJM’s Nominating 
Committee—which nominates Board candidates to be elected by the Members Committee—
includes three incumbent Board members (one of whom must not vote on the Nominating 
Committee) and five sectoral representatives. 34  This structure gives substantial influence to 
incumbent Board members and creates—even if unintentionally—a thumb on the scale favoring 
the status quo. Corporate governance scholars have long recognized that self-perpetuating board 
nomination processes can lead to detrimental entrenchment and insulation.35 Allowing only one 
incumbent Board member to serve on the Nominating Committee in a non-voting role would 
preserve information flows and representation of the current Board’s perspective in the nomination 
process while promoting true independence, responsiveness to PJM members, and bolder, more 
effective leadership. Notably, two ISOs—CAISO and ERCOT—have board nomination processes 
that provide no formal role for incumbent directors.36 
Ease restrictions on ex parte communications. Today, PJM’s Code of Conduct for its 
Board includes restrictive ex parte rules that limit the Board’s ability to communicate on important 
issues.37  These restrictions prevent the Board from effectively engaging with members and other 
 
34 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.1. 
35 See, e.g., Adolf A. Berle & Gardiner C. Means, The Modern Corporation and Private Property 88 (1932) (“[C]ontrol 
will tend to be in the hands of those who select the [nominating] committee by whom, in turn, the election of directors 
for the ensuing period may be made. Since the [nominating] committee is appointed by existing management, the 
latter can virtually dictate their own successors. Where ownership is sufficiently sub-divided, the management can 
thus become a self-perpetuating body even though its share in the ownership is negligible.”); Lucian A. Bebchuk, The 
Myth that Insulating Boards Serves Long-Term Value, 113 Colum. L. Rev. 1637, 1644 (2013) (“[A]rrangements that 
insulate boards from shareholders and shareholder pressure have been consistently associated with lower firm value 
and worse operating performance.”); Bo Becker & Guhan Subramanian, Improving Director Elections, 3 Harv. Bus. 
L. Rev. 1, 1 (2013) (“It is well known that U.S. director elections are largely a formality: incumbents typically 
nominate themselves, for elections that are almost always uncontested, and are re-elected with virtual certainty. The 
result … is what one might expect: directors who are elected not for their qualifications but rather because shareholders 
simply have no other choice.”). 
36 See CAISO Board Selection Policy § 4.2; Tex. Utils. Code § 39.1513(a), (d). 
37 PJM Board of Managers Code of Conduct at 3 (updated Nov. 2025).

13 
 
stakeholders on important issues. Nor are these counterproductive restrictions needed to protect 
the Board’s independence: No other RTO or ISO imposes such severe restrictions,38 and they do 
not fit the Board’s role: PJM under the Federal Power Act is a public utility, not a regulator, and 
we must not foster the misimpression that the Board is akin to another layer of regulation. PJM’s 
ex parte rules thus must be amended to eliminate or significantly reduce limits on communications 
between the Board and stakeholders. Reforming PJM’s ex parte rules would improve governance 
by enabling Board members to receive timely, balanced, and informed perspectives on complex 
reliability, market, and transmission planning issues. This reform, in particular, would assist the 
Board in considering innovative reforms necessary to move the grid forward. It will allow a freer 
exchange of new, innovative ideas from stakeholders—like AEP’s ALIGN concept—and from 
other RTOs who are also using integrated system planning and other techniques to cut through 
today’s load, transmission planning, and generator interconnection issues to provide solutions that 
more nimbly meet the needs of todays’ grid.  
 
38 See generally Christopher A. Parent et al., Exeter Assocs., Inc. Governance Structure and Practices in the FERC-
Jurisdictional ISOs/RTOs, Exeter Assocs., Inc. (Feb. 2021) (discussing PJM’s ex parte restrictions and not identifying 
any ex parte restrictions for other RTOs or ISOs), https://nescoe.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/ISO-
RTOGovernanceStructureandPractices_19Feb2021.pdf; see also MISO, Principles of Corporate Governance § V.E 
(Dec. 7, 2023) (providing that if “a third party [initiates] a communication directly with a Director on Board or 
Company business without notice to the other Directors,” the Director involved in the communication “shall promptly 
report the substance of the discussion to the CEO and to the full Board no later than its next regularly scheduled 
meeting.”).
